notes.meaning: Two members from the tribe of Levi, named Amram and Jochebed, married each other. This marriage took place within the same family line to keep the tribes of Israel distinct. God was quietly preparing the family that would bring forth Israel's rescuer.

Jochebed gave birth to a healthy, beautiful baby boy. His parents saw something special in him and believed God had a purpose for his life. Trusting God rather than fearing the king's cruel command, they managed to keep him hidden for three months.

When the baby could no longer be hidden safely, his mother built a small floating basket out of papyrus reeds. She coated it with tar and pitch to make it waterproof, placed her baby inside, and set it among the reeds along the Nile River. She committed her child to God's care where the water current would not sweep him away.

Moses' older sister, Miriam, stayed nearby and watched from a safe distance. She kept watch to see who might discover the basket and what would happen to the baby. Her watchful care showed both family love and hope that God would preserve the child.

The daughter of the king of Egypt went down to bathe in the Nile River while her servants walked along the bank. The river was considered sacred by the Egyptians, and royalty had private spots for washing. She spotted the floating basket among the reeds and sent her servant girl to fetch it.

When the princess opened the basket, she found the crying baby inside. The baby's tears touched her heart, and she felt deep pity for him. Even though she recognized that he was a Hebrew child whose life was forbidden, she chose to protect him.

Miriam acted quickly and approached the princess with great courage and wisdom. She asked if she should go and find a Hebrew nursing mother to care for the baby. This clever offer gave the princess an easy way to care for the child without public scandal.

Pharaoh's daughter told the young girl to go ahead and find a nurse. Miriam ran immediately and brought back the baby's own mother. God worked through ordinary family loyalty so that the mother could openly hold and care for her own child.

The Egyptian princess handed the child over to Jochebed and promised to pay her wages to nurse and raise him. Under royal protection, the mother was paid to care for the son she had risked everything to save. This surprising turn showed God's gracious reward for the parents' faith.

After the child was weaned and older, his mother brought him back to the palace, where the princess adopted him as her son. She named him Moses, explaining that she had drawn him out of the water. Growing up in the palace gave Moses the finest education and leadership training in Egypt, while his early years had grounded him in the faith of his people.

When Moses became a grown man, he went out to see the harsh treatment his Hebrew relatives were enduring. He chose to identify with his own oppressed people rather than stay comfortable in the royal court. While watching, he saw an Egyptian master beating a Hebrew worker.

Moses looked all around to see if anyone was watching, struck down the Egyptian, and buried his body in the sand. He acted out of genuine sympathy for his brother, but he moved in secret and in his own strength. His actions showed deep courage for his people, yet his timing was not yet aligned with God's plan.

The next day Moses went out again and saw two Hebrew men fighting each other. Grieved to see brothers hurting one another while already under cruel slavery, he challenged the one who started the fight. He urged the man to stop attacking his fellow countryman.

The guilty man angrily rejected Moses' correction, asking who had appointed him to be their ruler and judge. He brought up the Egyptian Moses had killed the day before, showing that the secret was out. Moses became terrified, realizing his deed was known and his position in Egypt was ruined.

When Pharaoh learned what Moses had done, he ordered him to be put to death. Moses fled from Egypt to save his life and traveled across the desert to the land of Midian. Arriving as a lonely runaway, he sat down to rest beside a community well.

A local priest and leader in Midian had seven daughters who came to the well to water their father's sheep. In that culture, daughters of desert leaders often did the daily work of tending and watering the family flocks. They drew water and filled the troughs for the animals to drink.

Rude shepherds came up and drove the young women away so they could take the water for their own flocks. Even though Moses was an exhausted stranger, he could not stand by and watch the weak being mistreated. He stepped in, protected the women, and helped them water their animals.

The daughters arrived back home much earlier than usual, surprising their father Reuel. He asked them why they had finished their chores so quickly that day. Their fast return revealed that the bullies at the well had been delaying them every single day.

The daughters told their father that a man dressed like an Egyptian had rescued them from the bullies. They added that he had even drawn water from the deep well himself and helped them finish watering the sheep. Because of his clothing and speech, they assumed he was an Egyptian traveler.

Reuel corrected his daughters for leaving such a helpful man sitting alone at the well. Desert hospitality required offering food and shelter to travelers, especially one who had protected them. He told them to find him right away and bring him home to share a meal.

Moses accepted Reuel's warm hospitality and agreed to stay and work with him as a shepherd. Over time, Reuel gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses to be his wife. The former prince of Egypt settled into a quiet, humble life in the desert.

Zipporah gave birth to a son, and Moses named him Gershom. The name means 'a stranger there,' reflecting Moses' feeling of living as an exile far from his true home. Even as he built a family, Moses never forgot that Midian was not his permanent dwelling place.

Many years passed, and the king of Egypt who had hunted Moses died. Yet the hard slavery of the Israelites did not end with the new ruler; their misery only deepened. In their deep suffering, the people groaned and cried out for help, and their desperate prayer rose up to God.

God heard the groaning of His suffering people. The Bible says He remembered His covenant, which means He began turning His active attention to fulfill His promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. His coming rescue was based entirely on His faithful word, not on anything the people had earned.

God looked down with pity upon the people of Israel and took personal notice of their pain. He knew their deep sorrow and decided the time had come to step in and save them. His silence had ended, and His plan of deliverance was now ready to begin.
